# RBAC matrix: what each seeded role may do

<!-- Generated by backend/internal/modules/identity/rbacmatrix_test.go. Do not edit by hand. -->

It is rendered from the permission documents the server writes into every new
workspace. To change a permission, change the seeded policy in
backend/internal/modules/identity/internal/policy/policy.go and regenerate this
page from the backend directory:

    go test ./internal/modules/identity/ -run RBAC -update

The same test runs on every build without -update and fails when this page and
the seeded values disagree.

## How to read the table

Each row is one kind of record the system governs. Each column is one of the
roles a new workspace starts with.

Every cell holds four positions, **C R U D**, always in that order:

- **C**: create a record of this kind
- **R**: read one
- **U**: update one
- **D**: delete or archive one

A letter means the role may do that. A dash in its place means it may not. So
CRU- is create, read and update but never delete, and ---- is no access at all.

**Row scope** is a second, independent question. It belongs to the role rather
than to a cell, so it is listed once per role below. The letters say what a
role may do to a *kind* of record; row scope says *which* records of that kind
it may write:

- **own**: only records the user owns.
- **team**: records the user owns and records owned by a teammate, resolved
  through live team membership.
- **all**: every record in the workspace.

Both questions have to pass, and they do not bind equally. Row scope narrows
writes. A customer record (contact, company, lead, deal, project) is read by
every seat that holds its read grant, whatever their scope. So a rep holding
CRU- on deals reads the whole workspace's deals and may update only the ones
their scope reaches, while a read-only auditor holding R--- reads them all and
changes none.

## The six roles a workspace starts with

| Role | Name in the app | Row scope |
|---|---|---|
| `admin` | Admin | all |
| `management` | Management | all |
| `manager` | Team Lead | team |
| `rep` | User | own |
| `read_only` | Read-only | all |
| `ops` | Ops / Integrations | all |

## What this page does not cover

The table answers one part of the access-control question. The sections below
cover the rest.

### Admin-only areas that have no row in the table

Some parts of the system are open to the admin role and to nobody else,
whatever the table above says:

- **User administration**: inviting someone, changing a colleague's role,
  deactivating or reactivating an account.
- **Privacy and GDPR work**: erasing a subject's data, and assembling the
  export that answers a subject-access request.
- **The audit log**: reading the record of who changed what.

For those areas the only question is whether the seat holds the admin role.

### An agent gets no more than a row here shows, and normally much less

A seat can lend their access to an AI agent by issuing it a passport. The
passport carries no role from this table. Its holder may do only what *both* of
these allow, at the moment of each call:

- the scopes written into the passport when it was issued, which are chosen for
  one job and are usually a narrow slice of what the seat can do; and
- the live permissions of the seat who granted it, re-read on every call. So
  changing that seat's role, or deactivating them, narrows or ends the agent's
  reach immediately, part-way through whatever it was doing.

An agent's real permission is the intersection of the two: never wider than the
row you are reading, and usually far narrower. Some actions narrow further
still: they wait for a human to confirm them before they take effect, and a few
are closed to agents outright.

### Sharing one record with one colleague

An individual record can also be shared with an individual user. That widens
*which* records they reach and leaves *what* they may do with them unchanged:
sharing a deal achieves nothing for a role whose deal cell reads ----.

### Hiding individual fields

A role can withhold single fields from the records it may otherwise read.
platform/auth decides it, so no read has to remember to ask on its own. The
mask covers the record reads, the filtered export and its preview, the
aggregates, the structured query and the audit history. The structured query
refuses a masked field as a predicate as it does as a sort, since filtering by
a value is reading it. The audit history withholds the field in both the before
and after images. A mask also takes the fields its own would be recoverable
from, so a currency never travels beside a withheld amount.

What an operator may configure is narrower than what a mask withholds, and the
catalog in migrations/testdata/maskable_fields.txt is the list. A commission
entry's tier is withheld because a partner mask reaches it, and nobody names
it separately: two configurations for one fact would let them disagree.

No seeded role carries a mask, so nothing on this page says "this role sees the
record but not the amount on it". An operator may still author a mask on a
custom role.

The deal, project and contract reads also report masked_fields through a
different mechanism. Each withholds a reference to another record the reader
may not open: a deal's company, partner and delivery; a project's company; a
contract's company, deal and delivery. That follows from the referenced
record's own visibility rather than from a role document, so a mask authored
on a custom role does not reach it.

Write authority does not lift it either, the way it lifts a role mask
conditioned on outside_write_authority: being allowed to change a contract says
nothing about being allowed to read the company it names. A contract is
admitted by its deal or its company, and that decides admission only. A reader
let in through the deal is still asked, per reference, whether they could open
what it points at.
